Investing.com -- Cybersecurity names gained ground on a global software alert while Meta declined and a fresh escalation in the Middle East pushed crude to highs.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

Here are Investing.com's stocks of the week:

Cybersecurity stocks

Cybersecurity names were among the week's strong performers after an emergency security update for PHP, the programming language used by roughly 70% of websites worldwide, triggered a global alert.

Two critical vulnerabilities disclosed this week could allow hackers to take remote control of affected servers.

The incident highlights a growing challenge, with artificial intelligence accelerating the discovery of software weaknesses while potentially making them easier to exploit.

Okta led the moves with a 14% gain over the week, followed by Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike, both up 11%, and Cloudflare, up 9%.

Meta Platforms

Meta fell 7% on Thursday and is down 9.1% over the week after Wednesday's post-close results, with a surprise plan to issue a new class of non-voting stock overshadowing stronger-than-expected third-quarter revenue.

The company's special committee said in its filing that the move was motivated not only by keeping CEO Mark Zuckerberg in California but also by "an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital," citing recent and anticipated raises at Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI to fund the same AI growth.

The committee added that while Meta has sufficient resources for current needs, it would be prudent to act before more companies absorb available capital in the market. The Class C shares are intended for equity offerings from time to time and could be available as early as the end of 2026.

Tesla and SpaceX

Tesla gained 4.6% over the week, and SpaceX added 0.6% after both reported results and confirmed they are examining a tie-up.

Each company has established an independent special committee to explore a potential merger, CEO Elon Musk said, emphasizing that while independent directors are actively evaluating the transaction, talks remain at an early stage with no guarantee of an agreement.

(Updates with index/price moves, macroeconomic data, and company/geopolitical news from the first paragraph.)

US equity indexes traded mixed as escalating geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices weighed on risk appetite, partially offsetting small gains in technology.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.2% to 52,255.1, and the S&P 500 declined 0.4% to 7,631.2 after midday Friday. The Nasdaq Composite was less than 0.1% higher at 25,988.3.

All but two sectors declined, led by consumer staples. Energy and technology were the only sectors to rise.

Fifteen of the 20 top-performing stocks in a category with a market capitalization exceeding $200 billion each were from technology, according to data compiled by Finviz. This tech outperformance represents a recovery, as Meta Platforms' (META) plans announced Thursday to increase capital expenditure by $5 billion at the bottom end of the range for 2026 and launch a new, non-voting share class to raise funds helped spark a sell-off in the so-called AI trade.

"Investors continued to assess the recent selloff in AI-related stocks, driven by concerns over the sector's substantial capital requirements," D.A. Davidson said in a research note. "Although the pace of the decline in technology stocks moderated, escalating geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices kept risk appetite subdued."

Saudi Aramco has ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified with the Iran-aligned Houthis, Reuters reported. Meanwhile, an oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain in the United Arab Emirates, the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said, according to the news report, without identifying the cause of the spill or the tanker involved.

The front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil contract jumped 3.8% to $103.29 per barrel, and global benchmark Brent advanced 3.1% to $116.62 per barrel.

"Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on the Saudis, Iran's threats to escalate the means of retaliation, and [President Donald] Trump's post about a week ago to 'finish the job' are all contributing to this sentiment," Derek Holt, head of capital market economics at Scotiabank, said in a note.

The rise in crude prices is adding to inflation concerns and reinforcing expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer, the D.A. Davidson note said.

US Treasury yields jumped in midday trading. The 10-year yield climbed 3.1 basis points to 4.98%, the 30-year rate advanced 2.4 basis points to 5.31%, and the two-year yield rose 5.1 basis points to 4.67%.

S&P Global's October flash reading of manufacturing conditions rose to 56.0 from 55.9 in September, versus the 55.5 forecast in a Bloomberg-compiled survey, indicating an expansion to a 53-month high.

The final reading in the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index for October stood at 48.0 from the 46.3 preliminary estimate, beating expectations for no revision in a Bloomberg-compiled poll. That print was below the 48.1 final reported in September. Respondents expected a 4.7% inflation rate over the next year and 3.5% annual inflation over the next five years, both up from 4.6% and 3.4%, respectively, in September.

Gold futures fell 1.3% to $4,008.20, and silver futures dropped 1.8% to $54.02.

What Happened?

Meta (META:NASDAQ) introduced a new class of non-voting shares on Wednesday to help pay for its AI push.

Meta stock rose more than 4% in pre-market trading yesterday as the company also beat revenue estimates and guided above expectations for the fourth quarter.

The new Class C shares arrive in January 2027, and shareholders will get one new share for each share they own.

That works like a two-for-one split. Meta says the shares can fund acquisitions and keep top talent while CEO Mark Zuckerberg keeps control.

Spending is the reason behind the move, given that Meta is pouring money into chips and data centers.

Capital spending for 2026 is now expected at $135 billion to $145 billion, while free cash flow was negative $2.12 billion in Q3. A year ago, FCF was positive $10.63 billion.

Revenue came in at $64.6 billion, and analysts expected sales at $63.37 billion. Q4 revenue is guided to $73 billion to $76 billion.

META Stock Revenue, EBIT and Free Cash Flow Estimates in Billion USD (TIKR)

Muse is the big story, given that more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada set up the AI product in a month and a half.

Zuckerberg said the goal is a network that grows more valuable as more people join. He added that Meta will try to make money from Muse "somewhat sooner" than usual because it costs more to run.

CFO Susan Li said AI businesses should add revenue in 2027 while Reality Labs losses should narrow to around $15 billion next year.

What the Market Is Telling Us About Meta Stock

Investors are rewarding the story behind the spending.

Analyst Jesse Cohen said the market has moved from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for a compelling product. Meta stock is getting credit for Muse and its new AI models.

Legal risks remain, and a New Mexico judge ordered a $25 billion penalty on Wednesday.

Earnings per share were $3.83. Without a $9.89 billion settlement charge, it would have been $7.40. Meta also warned of more youth-related trials in the U.S.

Arm Just Dropped 19% in a Month. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©Alma Grigorita's Images from Canva
Key Takeaways

Arm stock fell 19.8% in the past month (through Tuesday's close). It gave back a 17% jump on Sept. 21 tied to Meta's Muse AI agent, while the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.5%.

Most of the fall came on days the whole chip sector sold off, and Arm hasn't changed its guidance, so the drop looks like a better entry point than a month ago.

A judge still has to rule whether Qualcomm can stop paying Arm royalties for five years. Qualcomm's payments equal about half of Arm's operating income.

Arm reports its fiscal second quarter on Nov. 4 against revenue guidance of $1.38 billion, with the stock about 32% below the $291 mean analyst target.

Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) stock is down 19.8% in the past month (through Tuesday's close), while the Nasdaq 100 slipped just 0.5%. It's still up 102% in 2026, but it now sits 51% below its June high.

Most of the damage came on days the whole chip sector sold off. But two of the month's worries are Arm's own, and the bigger one hasn't been settled yet.

The Muse rally didn't last

On Sept. 21, Arm jumped 17% on hopes that Muse, the AI agent from Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ), would lift demand for CPUs, as AI stocks rebounded.

It didn't hold. On Sept. 24, the stock fell 7.9% after reports that SoftBank's Arm stake backs a $25 billion loan facility. Then on Sept. 28, it sank 8.7% as fears about AI safety after a breach hit chip stocks.

By Tuesday, Arm had given back that whole jump and then some, closing about 32% below where it ended Sept. 21.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Arm Holdings, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Arm Holdings' Analyst Ratings

October brought the jury, and more chip selling

Arm fell 6.5% on Oct. 8 as an OpenAI revenue report hit chip stocks. It fell 6.9% on Oct. 16 in a selloff over how AI gets financed, and another 4% on Tuesday after the South Korean neocloud Elice had a weak market debut.

Qualcomm (QCOM:NASDAQ) took its lawsuit against Arm to a jury in Delaware on Oct. 5. On Oct. 13, the jury found Arm breached its license by holding back software patches and tools. It also found that Arm interfered with Qualcomm's dealings with Meta.

The damages? $1 on each of those two claims.

The stock closed about flat that day, then fell 6.8% on Oct. 14.

The judge matters more than the jury

US District Judge Maryellen Noreika still has to rule on whether the breach lets Qualcomm stop paying Arm royalties for five years. Arm argues that clause is unenforceable.
